C004.subject: Raising the minimum wage
C004.object: aggregate unemployment among prime-age workers in low-wage sectors
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage aggregate unemployment among prime-age workers in low-wage sectors]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of minimum wage changes in U.S. states with flexible labor markets during economic downturns (e.g., the 2007-2009 recession), using synthetic control methods to estimate effects on prime-age employment in low-wage sectors. — Directly tests the hypothesis under the specified temporal and geographic qualifiers, leveraging variation in minimum wage policies and aggregate demand conditions.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage employment effects, focusing on studies that report elasticities of labor demand specifically for prime-age workers (ages 25-54) in low-wage sectors, stratified by economic cycle (low vs. high aggregate demand). — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the predicted negative effect is consistently observed in the relevant scope, and to quantify the role of demand elasticity.

[PATH:theoretical] Search-and-matching labor market model calibrated to developed economies with flexible labor markets, incorporating monopsonistic competition and endogenous labor demand elasticity, simulated under low aggregate demand scenarios. — Provides a causal framework to isolate mechanisms and test counterfactuals, clarifying whether the hypothesized reduction in unemployment is theoretically plausible given the qualifiers.

scope.domain: low-wage labor markets with high elasticity of labor demand

qualifier.temporal: during periods of low aggregate demand
qualifier.geographic: in developed economies with flexible labor markets

C005.subject: Raising the minimum wage
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage economic growth and reduced poverty]

[PATH:empirical] Cengiz, D., Dube, A., Lindner, A., & Zipperer, B. (2019). The effect of minimum wages on low-wage jobs. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 134(3), 1405-1454. — This study uses a border discontinuity design to estimate the employment effects of minimum wage increases across U.S. states, providing direct evidence on labor demand elasticity and potential poverty reduction in low-wage markets post-2008.

[PATH:empirical] Autor, D. H., Manning, A., & Smith, C. L. (2016). The contribution of the minimum wage to US wage inequality over three decades. Journal of Labor Economics, 34(S1), S123-S158. — This paper examines the long-run impact of minimum wage changes on wage distribution and inequality, offering insights into whether minimum wage increases lead to broader economic growth or merely redistribute income among low-wage workers.

[PATH:literature] Neumark, D., & Wascher, W. (2008). Minimum wages and employment. Foundations and Trends in Microeconomics, 3(1-2), 1-182. — This comprehensive review synthesizes decades of research on minimum wage effects, including studies focusing on high-elasticity labor markets, and helps adjudicate conflicting findings on growth versus job loss in the post-recession U.S. context.

scope.domain: low-wage labor markets with high elasticity of labor demand

C006.subject: Raising the minimum wage in counties with high business concentration
C006.object: a net decrease in aggregate unemployment only when the minimum wage increase is accompanied by targeted small-business subsidies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in counties with high business concentration a net decrease in aggregate unemployment only when the minimum wage increase is accompanied by targeted small-business subsidies]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental analysis of U.S. county-level minimum wage changes combined with small-business subsidy data from the Small Business Administration (e.g., 7(a) loan programs) during periods of low national unemployment (e.g., 2015-2019). — Directly tests the conditional claim by comparing counties with and without concurrent subsidies, controlling for business concentration, to isolate the net employment effect.

[PATH:theoretical] Agent-based simulation models of local labor markets with high firm density and low-wage sectors, calibrated to U.S. county data, incorporating minimum wage hikes and targeted subsidies to small firms. — Allows exploration of the causal mechanism (local multiplier effects, firm survival thresholds) under controlled conditions, testing the necessity and sufficiency of subsidies for net unemployment reduction.

scope.domain: low-wage labor markets with strong local multiplier effects and high firm density

qualifier.temporal: during periods of low national unemployment and stable small-business credit availability
qualifier.geographic: in U.S. counties with high business concentration

C007.subject: Raising the minimum wage
C007.object: increased aggregate unemployment due to higher labor costs and reduced hiring
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage increased aggregate unemployment due to higher labor costs and reduced hiring]

[PATH:empirical] Cengiz, D., Dube, A., Lindner, A., & Zipperer, B. (2019). The effect of minimum wages on low-wage jobs. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 134(3), 1405-1454. — This study uses a 'bunching' estimator across U.S. state minimum wage changes and finds no significant employment effects for low-wage workers, directly challenging the hypothesis of increased aggregate unemployment.

[PATH:empirical] Meer, J., & West, J. (2016). Effects of the minimum wage on employment dynamics. Journal of Human Resources, 51(2), 500-522. — This paper examines hiring and separation rates rather than just employment levels, showing that minimum wage increases slow hiring but do not raise unemployment, which would test the 'reduced hiring' mechanism in the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Neumark, D., & Wascher, W. (2008). Minimum Wages. MIT Press. — This comprehensive review presents the classic theoretical and empirical case for disemployment effects of minimum wages, providing a benchmark for evaluating the hypothesis, especially under the specified scope of low-profit-margin businesses and weak labor demand.

scope.domain: low-wage labor markets where businesses have low profit margins

qualifier.temporal: during periods of weak labor demand and low inflation
qualifier.geographic: in the United States and other advanced economies with similar labor market structures
